utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some small but possibly important issues after we have heard the case, if it could be called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ann Sutherland assisted by Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic assisted with Mr. Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was a little bit fast last Friday, only to be on the safe side, possibly repeating, I understood that the Defence has no chance during this week to have the necessary in-depth consultation with the client, and therefore is not able to give, if any, reactions to the remaining questions as to signatures and other documents not signed. And I take it, as far as the Defence has pointed out, that signatures are not contested on several documents, but to that end, the parties regard this as agreed facts. One other point is related to the application of Rule 92 bis. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has handed down, the 7th of June, a new decision clarifying some, until now, open questions on the application of this rule. It is only fair to give all the participants the chance to revisit the decision whether to tender or to consent to bring statements of witnesses under 92 bis into evidence. And therefore, I expect statements of -- given by the parties no later than Monday, 8 July, possibly we will have a clue why this date, Monday, 8 July, whether or not they can or one party comes to another decision under this new Appeals Chamber, decision of 7 of June. And I would ask the registry to distribute this to the parties and have it as Exhibit J5 for our case. Finally, from my point of view I have to tell you that due to urgent circumstances I just learned a few minutes ago, we can hear tomorrow only until 4.00 sharp. This concludes my introductory remarks for this morning. Any observations by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had promised Your Honour an indication of the position of my office as to the July schedule. I just wanted to indicate that the Prosecutor has been out of town, and she'll be back tomorrow so I won't have the decision until tomorrow or Wednesday probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Better tomorrow than Wednesday. Anything else? Then the witness may be brought in. It's our understanding it's a protected witness with face distortion and pseudonym. So the witness will be called Witness R. Are there any proofing notes for today necessary?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They should have been given to you at 8:30 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then would you please give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And let me please, first of all, before we start, apologise that here in the courtroom, you are not addressed with your family name but for your protection -- or in the interest of your protection, with the name Witness R. It's just for your protection. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then the OTP may start with the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown this piece of paper, passing it to the Defence before you show it to the witness, please. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, could the Defence please be shown that piece of paper before the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at that piece of paper and confirm whether that is your name without saying your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that piece of paper can be given to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It should have Exhibit Number S128. I can't see any objections from the side of the Defence. Therefore, admitted into evidence as S128.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session so that I can ask some background questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we've now moved into open session, so please take care not to give any information which may reveal your identity. If you need to do that, can you please ask to go into private session. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August 1991, did you join the reserve police force in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the commander of the Kozarac police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The commander of the police station in Kozarac was Didovic Osman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any heavy weapons situated in the Prijedor municipality; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, there were heavy weapons to be seen in Prijedor municipality, situated within the Prijedor barracks in Pasinac, not far from Prijedor, in the villages around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time period are we talking about, when you saw these heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That was when the war in Croatia began, that is, in Slovenia first, and then in Croatia. A lot of the weapons came from Croatia and Slovenia, weapons that then remained in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the Prijedor barracks, what was the predominant ethnicity of the persons living in those areas that you just mentioned where the heavy weapons were situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The population was predominantly Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the inter-ethnic relationships like between the Muslims and the Serbs, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, at that time when the war began and in view of the situation of Croatia, the situation became more complex. Following the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, every day, the situation became more and more complex. So at the time we're talking about, the relationship was not that good between Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When soldiers returned to the Prijedor municipality from the war in Croatia, do you know where they were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were located in Benkovac, that's close to Mrakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, what was situated at Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was sports complexes. We had a youth organisation there, a youth labour organisation in the building within that complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Benkovac from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Approximately 8 kilometres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit S14, which is the map of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take a moment to orient yourself with that map, and then if the map could be placed on the ELMO machine. Could you perhaps fold the map sufficiently so that you can see Kozarac and Benkovac on the map when it's placed on the ELMO machine. Could you please point to where Kozarac is on the map, on the ELMO machine to your right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Kozarac. This here, mainly this area here, this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to Kozarac town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you follow the road up to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This road here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned before, what was that place called where Benkovac was -- is situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was near Mrakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown photographs from S15. They are 003927 -- I'm sorry. The ERN number is 00392375, 00392397, 00392404, and 02147090, please. Could that be placed on the ELMO, 00392375.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In this photograph, you can see the town of Benkovac, which is where the army was located, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is depicted to the right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, you can see a stage where persons from the youth work force organisation organised festivals, that sort of thing, the stage on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the next photograph be put on the ELMO, 00392397.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Here you can see Benkovac. Facilities used for accommodation of those who would take part in the youth work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next photograph, 00392404.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 2402. We don't have...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. 02, 2402.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Here you can also see a part of this complex in Benkovac, these facilities that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, photograph 02147090. What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In this photo, we can see Benkovac, but it's a bird's eye view, probably taken from a plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the stage that you pointed out on photograph 00392375, does that appear on that photograph? And if so, could you please point to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it here, I think, on the right-hand side. I think that's it. This is the stage, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that on the grassed area to the right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it a square with -- brown square with white on the right-hand side of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If those photographs could be returned to the registry. Your Honour, do you want to mark them as exhibits now, give them numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Don't they have already numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, these don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if the registry could offer the new number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. The picture with ERN number ending 2375 is numbered S15/26. The picture with ERN number finishing 2397 is numbered S15/27. The picture with ERN number 2402 is numbered S15/28. And the ERN number 7090 is S15/29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then admitted into evidence under these numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you become aware of the behaviour of the soldiers at Benkovac towards the locals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. A bit further away from Benkovac, there was a place called Besce Poljana, the Besce field. There were a couple of Muslim families living there. In order to go to Kozarac, these families had to pass by Benkovac. So in March 1992, Eno Basic came to the police station in Kozarac accompanied by his wife, Fazila. They asked to see the police commander, Osman Didovic. As I was there outside the building, I showed them into the commander's office. And once inside the building, Eno Basic asked the commander Osman Didovic: "What sort of Chetniks are those people in Benkovac?" Osman immediately phoned the Prijedor barracks and talked to Radmilo Zeljaja. He asked him over the phone: "Zeljaja, what kind of army is it, the people there in Benkovac?" Whereupon he replied: "Well, Osman, I think you should come over. I'm not talking to you about this on the phone." Later on, the commander, Osman Didovic, told me: "Let's go to the barracks in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you pause there, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are now back in open session. Did you report for work on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of April, I reported for work. I went to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred that day when you arrived at work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When I entered the Kozarac police station, I found Muhamed Fazlic and Ekrem Besic there. They were both active-duty policemen. And the night before, they had been at the Prijedor police station. Their weapons were confiscated, and they were sent home, simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover, were checkpoints set up, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were checkpoints in Kozarac, for example, near the bridge in Kalata, near the church in Kozarac, at the crossroads on the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, at the entrance to Kozarac, all the places leading into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were manning these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were reserve policemen, active-duty policemen from Kozarac. There was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these persons manning the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was still mixed. There were still both Muslims and Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were these checkpoints set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Simply for security, out of fear that someone might come along and do something bad. Efforts were made to keep things under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any Serb checkpoints set up; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: From the time when the takeover took place, this was in Orlovci, in Kozarac near the petrol station on the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these persons at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I did. Goran Borovnica was often there. I saw Milos Preradovic on several occasions. Mile Jovic. These were people who had worked in Kozarac before that as active-duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Goran Borovnica an active-duty policeman in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, when the war broke out in Croatia, he went to the war front as a reservist, but he was a waiter by occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Branko Torbica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was an active policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the takeover, did you hear anyone from the SDA on the radio; and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I did. On Radio Prijedor, I heard Dedo Crnalic who had a catering establishment in Prijedor. Then Dr. Sadikovic, Muhamed Cehajic, the president of the municipality. And others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they saying? What was the gist of their conversations? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, mostly they were asking people to restrain themselves. They were promising that solutions would be found at a higher level. It was things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone from the SDS on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. They also spoke over the radio. There was Simo Drljaca, who then spoke of conditions under which things would function, that the Muslims were to hand over their weapons, and the non-Serbs as well. He was promising security for everyone. I heard him say those things. I also heard Mico Kovacevic, who was a doctor. Milomir Stakic, who at that time became the president of the municipality in Prijedor. Mostly they all used the same vocabulary. They spoke of the handover of weapons and of the conditions under which they would allegedly guarantee security in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Open session].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed that the transcript has frozen. We may need to take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would five minutes be enough?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the trial stays adjourned until 10.50. --- Break taken at 10.07 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we now continue with the examination-in-chief until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before the break, due to technical difficulties, I was requesting that we go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would like us to go back in private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Open session. Then we go. It is confirmed. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we are back into open session now. Just prior to the break, I asked you some questions in relation to hearing people on the radio, and you mentioned that you heard Milomir Stakic and Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people introduced on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: After the takeover, they were introduced as the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. And that's how they addressed the population, through the media, or Radio Prijedor at any rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover, did you attend a meeting at the Kozarac fire brigade building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this occurred? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This meeting was held in May, may have been the 13th or the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin who had arrived from Banja Luka and who was introduced as the head of the security services centre. Dule Jankovic, a commander from Prijedor. Cado, I'm not sure whether his name was Milomir. And the police in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to sign a pledge of loyalty to the new Serb government in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what was discussed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At this meeting, it was said that the Kozarac police should sign a pledge of loyalty, that the weapons should be turned in at places that were determined. It was that sort of thing mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Kozarac police sign loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: During the meeting, a major number of Kozarac citizens assembled, and the Kozarac police did not agree to sign the pledge of loyalty on that day, although the commander, Osman Didovic, in the name of what he called "peace" in Kozarac, he even tried to get people to take that step and to sign the pledge of loyalty. However, even the citizens assembling and a large number of policemen who just refused to go along with it, and the events that preceded this in other police stations, such as the one in Ljubija, so those who had signed the pledge of loyalty, everyone was fired. So at last, people refused to sign the pledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Stojan Zupljanin prior to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, no, I'd never met him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to another topic. What happened on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, at around 1300 hours, a radio connection was used by Zeljaja to call Osman Didovic, the commander of the police, and he told him to make sure that a military convoy was allowed to pass without any hindrance in the direction of Banja Luka. He made some conditions. He said what was supposed to happen. There were to be no armed people by the roadside. There were to be no obstacles. And Osman, the commander, accepted that. They concluded their conversation, after which I don't know how much time elapsed, but not very much, Zeljaja called again and told commander Osman Didovic that the convoy had been attacked in Jakupovici, and that he should go right away to see what was happening. At that point, Osman went toward his car. He was going to see what was going on when the shelling of Kozarac began, from several directions. It was so heavy that the commander had no possibility of checking what was actually happening. This went on until the next day, this shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the shelling continuous or intermittent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The shelling was continuous, continuous. It's hard to explain. Every second a shell landed. It was really intense, intense shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Zeljaja made radio contact with the commander of the Kozarac police station, Didovic. Where was Didovic stationed at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We were in Rizo [phoen] Kahrimanovic's house, this was in Dera, in Mrakovica on the left-hand side. After the meeting, this is where the Kozarac police station was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1992, did you see anybody killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, well, around an hour or two after the shelling started, there was an improvised hospital in the house where we were. Wounded people began to arrive. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I can't say exactly how many because there was chaos, and one didn't think of counting the people. But there were a lot, really, a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people that were seeing to these wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There was Dr. Jusuf Pasic, who before that had worked in the Kozarac hospital, and Azra -- I don't know what her last name was. But before that, she was a veterinary surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the shelling lasted until the next day. Can you tell the Court what happened the next day, that is, the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, 1992, after the intensive shelling, after a lot of people had been wounded, Dr. Jusuf Pasic and Dr. Azra arrived in the room where we were and begged Osman Didovic to try and to negotiate with Zeljaja so that at least the wounded could be taken to hospital in Prijedor. That was what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Osman Didovic negotiate with Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Osman Didovic established a radio connection with Radmilo Zeljaja. We were all there. We heard the conversation. Radmilo Zeljaja started at once spelling out the conditions under which he wanted Kozarac to surrender. Before that, commander Osman Didovic told him: "I'm here with a lot of wounded people, and there are some Serbs among them." His reply was: "There are no Serbs left in Kozarac." Then he said again: "But Vaso is here." He used to be a forester, a man who looked after the forest, and he was among the wounded. But Zeljaja insisted. He was ruthless. He insisted that the police from Kozarac should stand at the head of a column, with white flags raised high, that the wounded should go in front and the people should go behind the police. He insisted on this, and he kept saying: "You have to raise white flags. You have to raise them up high."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people of Kozarac surrender on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of May, along with everything I said, what Dr. Pasic and Azra had asked, it was decided that Kozarac should surrender, and all the conditions that Zeljaja had set up were met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Becir Medunjanin also attempt to negotiate with Zeljaja on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the building where we were, Becir Medunjanin arrived from somewhere. And he tried to talk to Zeljaja. I remember he told him that a delegation from Kozarac had already gone to Prijedor and had not come back. But mostly, the conversation boiled down to Zeljaja repeating what he had already said to commander Osman. After that conversation, Becir Medunjanin left that place and went off somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was part of this delegation that had gone to Prijedor to try and negotiate with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I know that Islam Bahonjic was in the delegation. I can't recall. I don't know the names of the others exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened on the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, 1992, the conditions were that a column should set out from Kozarac, the wounded in front, and the police and the people, along the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road in the direction of Prijedor to the bus stop called Limenka. And this was done. We set out on the 26th. When we arrived at the checkpoint at the bus stop called Limenka, we were met by soldiers in a lot of different uniforms. They were Serb soldiers. There were different kinds of weapons there. As we were moving along, we could see houses burning. They were burning around us. And when we got there, they started separating the men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were gathered at the Limenka bus station, bus stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It's hard to estimate, but in my estimation, about a thousand people, maybe more, who had gathered together on that day to surrender, and who followed the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were soldiers in a lot of different uniforms. Can you describe the uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were people in the usual olive-grey military uniforms. Then people in blue camouflage uniforms, also in olive-grey camouflage uniforms. There were black uniforms with Chetnik insignia on the caps. So they were of different kinds and colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone from -- did you recognise any policemen that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, at the checkpoint there were Milos Preradovic, Milo Jovic, Brane Bolta, Brane Torbica. At one point, he approached commander Osman. We were standing there and he said: "That bus down there, that's for the police." It was parked opposite Osman Kahrimanovic's house, about a hundred metres away from the checkpoint where we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people, of the thousand or so people that you saw at Limenka bus stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were Muslims. Muslims, with maybe an odd Croat among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the soldiers and police, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The policemen were Serbs, and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw houses burning in the vicinity. What village or villages were these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: From that place, you can see the village of Brdjani, part of Kozarusa. It was the surrounding villages that were burning, you could see those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the persons who lived in those villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation like at that time before -- before you were taken on to the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The situation was -- well, I could recognise it at once. They started maltreating people, taking them out of the column. There was shooting. At one point, from the place where I was standing, I saw Senadin Sara taken out. He used to be in Prijedor, but he happened to be in Kozarac on that day. Vlasim Besic, a plumber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw Mile Jovic and two other men in uniform taking them in the direction of the house that was at the roadside. It belonged to Zajko who was a Roma by ethnicity, a gypsy, a man who was working in Germany at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mile Jovic. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform with a white belt. It was an olive-grey camouflage military uniform of the kind worn by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S14, the map of the area, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to point out on the map where the village of Dera is located, and also Kozarusa, in relation to the town of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I didn't hear you very well. Kozarusa and?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dera. Where the police station was, on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Dera, Dera. Yes. The village of Kozarusa was here. And Dera was here in the direction of Mrakovica, right here. Before the village of Rajkovici, right here, in this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing on the map the road leading north out of Kozarac towards Mrakovica, and you say that the village of Dera is near Rajkovici on the left-hand side, is that correct, on the left-hand side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Dera from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: About 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You pointed a moment ago to Kozarusa. In what direction from Kozarac is Kozarusa? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many kilometres from Kozarac is Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Kozarusa is a kilometre and a half from Kozarac in the direction of Prijedor, that's where it is. About a kilometre and a half or 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to Brdjani, where you mentioned that saw houses burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Brdjani, it's this area here. When you go from Kozarac in the direction of Debeli Brijeg, where before the war there was a hut in the mountains for hikers. That's where Brdjani is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the right of Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If the map can be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a moment ago that there were some buses at the Limenka bus stop, and you were told that one of these buses was for the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many buses did you see at Limenka bus stop that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On that day, there were a lot of buses coming from Prijedor, from the direction of Prijedor, about 20. And the people were getting on, women and children on one set of buses, and the men on another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of buses were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were buses belonging to the Prijedor transport company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of these buses? Do you recall the name of the transport company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Autotransportno Brdezacji Prijedor. That was its name. It was in charge of public transport before the war. We used to refer to it as "Autotransport," "Autotransport Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ordered on to one of these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Torbica pointed out a bus that was designated only for the police from Kozarac, and that's the bus we boarded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone as you were going to the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As I was getting on the bus, right next to the bus, a dead man was lying on the ground face down, wearing a military olive-grey uniform. We passed by him as we were getting on the bus. And when we boarded the bus, Goran Borovnica got on. He had a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher. He was carrying an automatic rifle in his hand. He boarded the bus, and the first thing he said was: "Didn't I tell you that Kozarac would be Serbian?" We kept quiet. He started on us one by one. I was sitting there with Hajrudin and Muhamed Fazlic. He said: "Oh, you didn't beat me. You didn't beat me." And then he hit Nihad, and he said to him -- with his rifle butt, and he said: "You did beat me." And then he went toward the back of the bus. At one point, he called out: "Osman Didovic is here, the commander is here." And he went back and got off the bus right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They took us to the Prijedor SUP, behind the SUP building in Prijedor where there were garages, mostly behind the SUP building. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When we arrived there, I saw Djuro Karanovic, Bosko Grabez, Branko Bolta, Strika, they were all active policemen. They were all insulting us, cursing us, calling us "balija." Insulting us, abusing us verbally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a photograph from S15 with the ERN number 00392212, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You can see the Prijedor SUP here, where we were brought. The back of the building, but this is the entrance to the SUP building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that photograph can be returned to the registry. Your Honour, do you want to give it an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this photo is admitted as -- the former 4A is admitted into evidence as S15/31.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think it's 32, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We had in the meantime another one? Yes, right. 32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained at the SUP, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They took us -- they took two men, two by two, out of the group, and they didn't come back. First, we thought they were killing them or that something was happening to them, because they were taken away and they didn't come back. When it was my turn and the turn of Emir Sinanagic, who used to work in the Prijedor SUP as a forensic technician before, they took us into the lobby of the SUP building. A man I didn't know was sitting there, registering our names, saying that we had handed in our weapons, taking away our identification papers, and then we went out of the building through the front door, and there was a car waiting for us there. It was a Lada Niva car, a terrain vehicle. And then they took us in the direction of Urije. At the traffic lights, he turned right, came out on to the Prijedor/Banja Luka asphalt road, set out in the direction of Banja Luka, and then turned off just as we were approaching Keraterm and stopped there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When we arrived there, I went into the first garage. When I entered, there were about 50 people there already. I recognised the president of municipality, Muhamed Cehajic. He was sitting in a corner. Islamo Bahonjic was there, too. Muhamed Ergelic, also known as Cuko, who owned a pizzeria in Prijedor. The imam from Kozarusa, from Donja Kozarusa, was there, too. I think his last name was Granov. Many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any guards at the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. The guards were just outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were mostly wearing camouflage uniforms or military olive-grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw Muhamed Cehajic. What was his condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was obvious that he had been beaten. I noticed, after I came in, that his nails and fingers were blue from the beating. You could see that he had been beaten before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a photograph from S15, 02006269, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution's intention also to present at the same time 65 and 16, the two following in the binder, just to have it in order?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, 6265 is already exhibit 15/1. I can show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, and also please, once again, 2416.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we have it together. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness also be shown 02006265 and 02002416. 6269 is 8A on the index, 6265 is 8B, and 2416 is 8C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at the photograph 02006269, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You can see the Keraterm camp and the Keraterm building where we were brought from the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point on the ELMO machine to your right where you were first taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: To this garage here. Right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the room at the very end, on the left-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next photograph 02006265, which is Exhibit S1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You can see Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last photograph, 01002416.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, this is Keraterm also.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purposes of the admission into evidence, first of all any objections by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the former 8/1, the number ending with 69, will go under S15/33. Admitted into evidence. I understood that 8B is already admitted into evidence. And 8C, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. C is admitted as S15-34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was tendered as 34. And thereby admitted as S15/34. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you stay in the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I spent there the night between the 26th and the 27th. On the 27th, in the morning, empty buses arrived and parked outside but within the camp. In the evening hours, we were ordered to get on these buses. They didn't tell us where they would take us. So in the afternoon hours, around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, I couldn't tell, they began to load people on to these buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We were taken to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted on these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, were you told by the escorts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We were told to keep our heads down, as on our way there. Obviously they were insulting us as usual. But we were told to keep our heads down at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was your escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I don't. I didn't recognise any of the guards who were with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were from the police or the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think they were from the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Omarska from Keraterm? How many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: If you take the asphalt road, the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, perhaps about 28 kilometres, up to 30. I can't say with any precision, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you left Keraterm at around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. in the afternoon. What time did you arrive in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In the morning. I have to tell you again, time was not an issue for us. There was no need to look at our watches. We didn't even know what day it was. We lost all sense of time. But when we got to Omarska, it was morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from late afternoon until the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the buses going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I didn't know the route because I never took that route to go to Omarska, although I did go to Omarska quite often. But I didn't recognise the route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were there that left Keraterm for Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It's difficult to say really, because I got on to one of the buses, but there were many buses there, quite many. I only got on to one of these buses, and we were told to keep our heads down. So I didn't really have an opportunity to count the buses; I couldn't tell. But there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There must have been between 50 and 60 people on the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When we arrived in Omarska, you could hear sounds of shooting. You could hear the sounds of glass breaking. The electricity was cut off, and then on and off. The bus on which I was came there, parked outside a building. I didn't know what the building was used for. The electricity was turned back on at that moment. We were ordered to get off the bus. I was in the third seat on the right-hand side of the bus. Hajrudin Jakupovic was the man who sat next to me. Zilhad Hodzic was in front of me. Muhamed Ergelic, also known as Cuko. We started to get off the bus. There was a large group of uniformed persons waiting for us outside the bus. They were also wearing camouflage uniforms. At that moment, I saw Miroslav Kvocka standing there. I recognised him. Mladjo Radic, called Krkan, and many other uniformed persons. When we got off the bus, I saw that Muhamed Ergelic, Cuko, had been taken away. They -- these soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms took him by the arm and took him away. When Zilhad Hodzic came along, he was sitting in front of me, I heard that Mladjo Radic, also known as Krkan, told him: "Oh, commander, so you're here, too." And then they took him away, too. Hajrudin Jakupovic remained in front of me, but then they took him away, too, in the direction of the red house. When it was my turn, one of the soldiers asked: "Who killed Macola?" I just shrugged my shoulders. I thought they were going to take me away, too. I just put my hands up in the air. They grabbed hold of me, they took my jacket off, and ordered me to get inside the room. I entered by the door, climbed up a flight of stairs, and on the right-hand side, there was a red door, an iron door. I entered the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back over and ask you some questions in relation to the last answer you gave. You mentioned a man called Zilhad Hodzic, and you said that they said: "Oh, the commander's here." What was he a commander of, and what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was not a commander really. He used to be a commander at the police station in Omarska before the war, after which he worked in Prijedor. I'm not sure exactly what his work was, but he was one of the commanding staff in the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned when you first got off the bus you saw Miroslav Kvocka and Mladen Radic. Dealing with these people separately, first of all Kvocka, how long had you known him for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I'd known him for a long time. He'd come over to see me occasionally. He worked as a policeman at the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many years had you known him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Difficult to say. For a couple of years maybe, that's prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladen Radic, how long had you known him for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I'd also known him for quite a long time. He was also a policeman in Omarska. He'd come over to see me in the same period as Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the buses arrived in the morning. Do you know approximately what time in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I can't say really. It was in the morning. It dawned soon, and the new day came. That's how I could tell. But I didn't really look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, the buses, where were they from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The buses were coming from the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's my question. Do you know what type of buses these were that took you from Keraterm to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Those were also Autotransport Prijedor buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that soldiers ordered you to go into a room. Do you recall the number of that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know the number, but later I found out that it was Room Number 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a photograph from S15 with an ERN number 00409592, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, this is S15/18. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In this photograph, you can see the Omarska camp, the place we were taken to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pointing to the ELMO machine on your right, can you point to where the buses stopped when you arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Here, outside this gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the long red building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Room 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Room 15, after you entered this door, then up a flight of stairs, and then on the right-hand side. There's a flight of stairs there, and then on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If that photograph could be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you detained in Room 15 the entire time you were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was only in July when I was taken to be interrogated I spent one day at the pista, the area outside. Because when I was brought back from the interrogation, we were ordered to lie face down on the ground in that area. It was very hot outside. Emir Sinanagic was lying next to me. And prostrate like that, face down, he told me: "I'll ask Neso to take us back to Room 15." I approved of this because I realised that in this area outside, conditions were even worse. People were lying there face down. And then this really happened. He did eventually ask Neso to allow us to go back to Room 15, and on the evening on the same day, Neso indeed took us back to Room 15 where I spent the remaining time in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of the person you've referred to as Neso?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: His name was Nenad Janjic, nicknamed Neso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He was a guard there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the photograph S18 again, please. I should have had you do this when you looked at the photograph a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point out for the Court the pista area, where you said that you stayed for one day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On that day, I was taken to be interrogated in this building here where the restaurant was. It was on the first floor that I was interrogated. And then three policemen escorted me, and I was ordered here in this area between the building where the interrogation took place and this other building, I was ordered to lie down on the ground. There were a number of inmates there already. I was told to lie face down on the ground, and everyone I found there was lying in the same position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the area between the building that you've called the restaurant building and the long red building. Is that correct, as the pista area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the building in -- at the front of the photograph? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: You mean this one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This is the white house. That's how we referred to it. Although I'd say "black house" would be a more appropriate name. However, we did call it "white house".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other building on the far right-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This one, we used to call it the red house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a name that you had for the long red building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: We called it the hangar. There below, camp inmates were accommodated. But before, there were iron ore mine facilities there inside, and heavy machinery used in the mines, so that's perhaps why it was called "hangar".

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that photograph could be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you were interrogated. Do you recall the people that interrogated you, the names of the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Zare Tejic. Babic was the last name of the other person. I don't know his first name. But they both used to work in the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what positions they held? Prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think they were investigators. Zare Tejic was first a policeman, and then an inspector, but I know they both worked in the SUP. I knew them because they would often come to my catering establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during your detention at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Maltreatment was constant. They were plundering. They were taking away our watches. Everything we had on us, leather jackets, rings, they were beating us. They were calling out our names. They kept provoking us all the time in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: This occurred between the 18th and the 20th of June. Again, it was difficult to tell which time it was. Time ceased to matter for us. But I think that it was in that period because (redacted) (redacted) And it was maybe a week after that. In the evening hours, around 11.00 in the evening, my name was called out, and I was afraid that the same thing would happen to me as had happened to others because if anyone came back at all, then at least they had been badly beaten. So at first, I decided not to respond. But when they called my name again, I heard a voice saying: "Nothing will happen to you. There's a parcel here for you." So I decided to come out. I reached the gate, and there outside Nenad Janjic, Neso, was waiting for me, and Vlado Kobas was with him. Vlado Kobas was holding a nylon bag. He gave it to me and said: (redacted) (redacted) Then he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. turned around and left. At that moment, Nenad, Neso, Janjic told me: "Come with me, so you can have your meal in peace." I followed him from Room 15 down the corridor, and there on the left-hand side there was an office with "police" written on the door in Cyrillic letters. I entered the room, and I asked him: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Then he took me with him. He told me to follow him. I left the office and headed for Room 19 and then down the stairs. Then he asked me: "Where's your car? Where's your money? Where did you hide it?" As we knew each other well, I tried to explain that I had been building a house of my own, so I had no money left, at which point he hit me very hard, and then he dealt another blow. I fell down the stairs after the first blow. Ure also took part in this. "He also told me, Ekrem Melkic also, told me that there was no money. And I took him away, he suddenly had some, but that's why he's dead today." Then I fell down, and he ordered me to stand up. I stood up. He took me towards the exit, the door I came in when I entered the camp first. We left the building, and he shouted: "Krkan, Krkan, what shall I do with this man? I just found him. When shall we leave?" And he answered: "Tomorrow. Can't you see I'm busy now?" Zeljko Meakic, the commander of the camp, was also there. I also saw Miro Solaja, who was lying on the ground, and a bit further down, I saw Silvo Saric, who was being beaten. Then Milorad Tadic, called Brk, ordered me to go back to Room 15. But he warned me not to try to escape because tomorrow, they would be there for me to take them to my house and give them the money I had hidden there. After I returned to Room 15, I decided to try to hide. So I was no longer in the room in which I had been, but there two other rooms under this one. At the entrance to the building on the left-hand side, there were two washbasins, cement washbasins, and I decided just to squat under one of these and not to respond when they called my name. They did call my name out twice afterwards, but I didn't respond. I was only saved by my good luck. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, out of an abundance of caution, whether we need to make a redaction at 12.03.40 and following, in relation to the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. It may be redacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you -- in the last answer that you gave, were you referring to (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw two people at the exit of the hangar building, Silvo Saric. What position did he hold in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I think he was the president of the Prijedor HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miroslav Solaja? Forgive my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Miroslav -- Miro Solaja, we used to call him Miro, he was a driver for the Prijedor Football Club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you had been beaten by Milorad Tadic, otherwise known as Brk. How long had you known this person for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, for quite a long time actually. He worked in the Agriunija, agricultural union in Kozarac. On the way out of Kozarac, if you take the road to Trnopolje, this Agriunija community was on the left-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known him for? Approximately how many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Quite long. Perhaps 7, 8, maybe 9 years. Anyway, I'd known him for a long time. We go back to the time when he worked at the Agriunija, and then he used to be a taxi driver in Omarska. So he came quite often to my house also, and we knew each other quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the man, the other man, who was with Milorad Tadic otherwise known as Brk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I saw him for the first time in Omarska. And he was a guard in Nenad Janjic's, Neso, shift. They called him Ure. That is, Brk referred to him that night as Ure. He had a limp in one of his legs. He was an older man really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they beating you with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: What were they beating us with? Mostly they kicked us with their military boots. Ure beat me with some sort of a rod, or more like a baseball bat. It was made of wood. He was carrying a length of thick, industrial cable in his hand. And there was a piece of iron tied to one end of this industrial cable to beat prisoners with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a permanent injury from this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I have some injuries on my left leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a scar from the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long is the scar, and how wide?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It's about 11 or 12 centimetres long and about 3 centimetres wide, 3 and a half maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, were all the redactions caught in relation to the witness's sister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw Silvo Saric, the president of the HDZ party, and Miroslav Solaja. What did you see happening to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw that they had been beaten. Miro Solaja was lying unconscious beside a pillar. I saw Zeljko Meakic beating Silvo Saric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known Zeljko Meakic for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Not really for a very long time. But he also used to come to my catering establishment. We were not really close. He used to come to my restaurant sometime with his friends, so that's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any corpses in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That day, when there was, as they used to call it, breakfast, groups of between 20 and 30 people went out of Room 15 to have breakfast, and then we were not allowed to immediately return to Room 15. But we had to finish up breakfast -- and it was a kind of meadow -- before we were allowed to return to the room. At one point, we were suddenly ordered to keep our heads down. When I heard this order, of course, we all kept our heads down. But out of sheer curiosity, I didn't keep my head all the way down so I could see that from the direction of the red house, there was a TAM truck arriving. It was a yellow TAM truck, driven by Vlado Kobas. With him in the car were another two people. The vehicle passed us by. And as it drove by, I saw Islam Bahonjic's dead body, and Muharem Kahrimanovic's dead body, who was a driver for the Celuloza company. I recognised these two bodies because they were lying on top of the heap. I didn't recognise the other bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Islam Bahonjic's occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Before the war, Islam Bahonjic was an x-ray technician. And he worked in the Prijedor hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vlado Kobas, what was his occupation before the war, the driver of the vehicle -- the TAM truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Before the war, Vlado Kobas worked in the Omarska mine, in the company where we were, in fact, kept prisoner. I got to know him because he used to, when I had built my new house, he built a part of the construction, something to do with drainpipes. And that's when I actually met him for the first time. He used to come to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the condition of the bodies of Islam Bahonjic and Muharem Kahrimanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: As far as I could see, I didn't dare raise my head to take a good look, but I could see that they were dead bodies, bodies that had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any dead bodies near the white house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. You could see -- sometimes they would take us to the toilet outside Room 15, up near the white house. And then you could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you see dead bodies near the white house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Often. When we went to have the so-called breakfast, while we were queuing up, we could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another topic, so this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this morning, you mentioned in your testimony that when you first arrived at Omarska, there were a number of people that were taken away, Hajrudin Jakupovic, Zilhad Hodzic, and Muhamed Ergelic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you first got off the bus, you saw Kvocka and Radic. Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of people there I didn't know. Uniformed persons, persons wearing camouflage uniforms. Upon entering Room 15, I found out that they were civilian police, that's what they called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these persons belong to any particular group that you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I only heard that there were paramilitary units there who were neither the police, nor the army proper. That was before the takeover in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also before we broke for lunch, in reference to the white house, you said a more appropriate name would be "black house." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In the white house, every day, you could see people being beaten as we were on our way to lunch, they would bring people to the white house. Once I saw that Becir Medunjanin was among the people being brought there. And many other people, too. The horror that took place in the camp, probably most of it took place in the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the conditions in Omarska camp, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conditions in relation to food, water, hygiene.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: These conditions are very difficult to describe because the conditions as such were not there. This word would have been pointless in the Omarska camp. There were no conditions. It was like animals, perhaps even animals would have been treated better. There were no hygiene facilities. We were taken to eat once a day. The time we were given to eat was two minutes. You had to run to the kitchen, while being beaten and hit. On the way back, you were being beaten again. There was no health care, no medical attention. It's just quite difficult to describe such conditions and how man could survive that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you provided with water to drink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Sometimes they would give us water. Most often, we had no water. Even if they gave us some, it was usually water with a special flavour, probably water taken from the hydrant, industrial water. Certainly not drinking water. So we didn't really have enough water either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone from the Serb authorities in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp, no, I didn't see any of them there. Because on that day, we didn't leave Room 15. But I heard that Simo Drljaca, Brdjanin, Zeljaja, Arsic, Kupresanin did visit the camp. This was the group of people who visited the camp. But I must say again that I did not see them myself; I just heard that they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Drljaca in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I saw him in the camp twice. That's in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The first time I saw him, it was at lunchtime. We were lined up. We were about 30 people there waiting to have lunch in the restaurant. He was standing near the restaurant with a woman. That was the first time I saw him. The second time, it was also within the camp. He was there with Zeljko Meakic, and I noticed that Zeljko Meakic was carrying some papers in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known Simo Drljaca for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Prior to the war, perhaps for two or three years. Usually I'd meet him at Aco Ostojic's [phoen] catering establishment in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Simo Drljaca did before the takeover, what his occupation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was a lawyer. He worked in education. He worked with schools, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to another topic. Do you know a person called Said Dzihic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Did you say Said Dzihic, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Fikret Balic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were with me in Room 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if they were called out of Room 15 at the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It was perhaps the 24th or the 25th of July. I think it was on the 24th or the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they say to you upon their return to the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: When they returned to Room 15, Said Dzihic told me that he had been loading dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention how many bodies and where he was loading the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He said that there had been around a hundred dead bodies. They had loaded these bodies on to a lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say where these bodies were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He told me that he had recognised Dr. Jusuf Pasic's body. Zijad Mahmuljin, who had been the manager of the sawmill in Kozarac. Ilijaz Jakupovic, nicknamed Ilko. He said that he had been able to recognise these bodies, but that he couldn't identify the other bodies. He said he had seen some terrible things, bodies with severed heads, bodies mutilated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he was loading these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: In the red house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it that you remember this date, the 24th or the 25th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Well, you know, from the very first to the very last day in the camp, we had a really, really difficult time. But on those particular days of July, around the 24th and the 25th, there was some sort of a catharsis. Names were being called out all the time. The things that happened at that time were things that hadn't happened at the camp previously. This period was probably the period of cleansing. They were cleansing part of the people there.
