So that's why I still remember these two dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the 6th of August, 1992. You said that you were detained in Omarska up until that date. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the first day, names were called out since the morning hours. Zeljko Meakic was reading names out from a list. No one told us where we were headed to. Those whose names were called out had to get on to buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your name called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got on the buses, where did you go? I'm sorry. Approximately how many buses did you see in the Omarska camp that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There may have been about 50 buses inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, what sort of buses were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Those were also Autotransport Prijedor buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were put on the bus, where did the bus go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The buses left. And on the buses, people were being maltreated by the escorting police. They ordered us not to watch out of the bus windows. There were lots of us on the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: There were about, perhaps, 80 people. It was a busload, and we weren't seated. We had to lie down, but the bus was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you leave the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any escorts on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I did recognise a number of them when we reached Manjaca, the Manjaca camp. But in the bus that I was on, I recognised none of the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of uniform -- I'm sorry. How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The ones that I saw there, and the ones that I could recognise, I saw Brane Bosnjak, the policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: They were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the Manjaca camp, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Sometime after midnight. Between midnight and early morning. We didn't have our watches on us. It had all been taken from us, watches and other personal belongings in Omarska. So it must have been sometime after midnight the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Manjaca, did you witness anyone being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Names were being called out again. Nezir Krak, the car mechanic from Prijedor was also called out. Dedo Crnalic. Names were being called out until daybreak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to either of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, they never got out alive. They never left the camp, and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you -- when were you released from the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: On the 18th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your release, besides the international Red Cross, did anyone else visit the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion in Manjaca, Brdjanin came. In this stable where I was, where we were, he spoke to us. He was escorted by the camp commander -- deputy camp commander, a man we called Spaga. He spoke to the inmates that time, and he said: "Serbian prisoners get a very different treatment." What we have is more like a hotel. And he said they were trying to ensure our release and our transport to third countries. And the whole situation, whatever was happening to us, he said: "Alija Izetbegovic, the government, and the SDA were to blame." Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that it was Mr. Brdjanin that addressed the detainees in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin was a difficult man not to know. He often appeared in the media, on the television. He was a very high-ranking SDS politician. So I simply knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he often appeared in the media, on television. What did you hear him say on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Whenever he spoke, at least, the ones I witnessed, although I had little time to follow the events, but it really was a period that boded ill. So there was general interest in what was going on and the statements that were made. Most often, he used expressions like "Turks." He called Muslim people Turks. He said their place was not here. He emanated a sort of negative energy in all his appearances, which did not help the inter-ethnic relations at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him on television, what time period is this? 1992 or prior to 1992, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Ever since the first multiparty elections, the preelection rallies from 1991 onwards, all the leading figures from the three nationalist parties often appeared on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you specifically recall seeing him in the first five months of 1992 prior to your detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember now, and I can't say with any degree of certainty the period, whether it was five months earlier or later. I really can't recall, but these appearances were quite frequent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to another topic -- I'm sorry, before I do that, can you make a comparison between the conditions in Omarska and the conditions in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Manjaca, too, was a camp. But after the International Red Cross came, the situation improved really. As I've often said myself, it was luxury compared to Omarska, although, Manjaca, too, was a camp and there were stables there where cows and sheep had been kept. But to compare Omarska and Manjaca, that's after the Red Cross had arrived, the difference was really huge in favour of Manjaca. Manjaca was a much safer place. People weren't taken out of their -- out of their accommodation facilities at night to be beaten. Nothing like that ever happened in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to another topic. Can you please tell the Court the names of any of the policemen that you know were killed in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I'll try to remember all of them. That is, all of those whom I knew. Muhamed Fazlic was one of them. Hajrudin Jakupovic. Mirsad Alic. Esad Alic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the person -- do you know a person by the name of Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, Emir Karabasic. It's very difficult for me to remember all of them at this moment. Yes, you're right, Emir Karabasic was also one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muhamed Jakupovic, do you know a person by that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, Muhamed Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I am not entirely sure, although I know Muhamed Jakupovic very well. He used to be a traffic policeman and was originally from Kamicani. I cannot tell you for sure whether he was or wasn't. I think he was, but again, I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Zilhad Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Zilhad Hodzic. I believe I mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ibrahim Denic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Braco, yes. We used to call him Braco. That was his nickname, yes, Ibrahim Denic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, he was. On that night, he entered Room 15 together with me. But shortly after that, he was called out, maybe half an hour later. And I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber the names of people you know who have been missing since 1992, policemen, the names of policemen who have been missing since 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: The names of the policemen whom I knew went missing are Emir Karabasic, Muhamed Jakupovic, Muhamed Fazlic, Ekrem Besic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of -- I'm sorry. Continue. What was the name you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Klipic. It's a family name. He was from Jakupovici. I don't know his family name. He was also an active police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Edin Besic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Edin Besic, Boca we used to call him. His nickname was Boca. He was also from Kozarac. Osman Didovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Emsud Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Emsud Bahonjic, yes, he was with the reserve police force. Akib Deumic, also a member of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Edin Mujagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Edin Mujagic, yes, a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The names that you've just mentioned, did they all disappear in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: To this date, none of these reappeared, which means that they all went missing in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to other people that weren't policemen who either died or went missing in 1992. Can you please name them. And if you know the circumstances of their fate, can you please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: (redacted) He disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to break for a moment. And please redact from page 59 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Line 19?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Line 19 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any other persons that either died or went missing in 1992 besides your relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: I have already mentioned some of them. Omer Mahmuljin is not related to me. Hamdija Avdagic also. He was also from Kozarac. Jusuf Muretcehajic. It really is a long list. The only problem is that at the moment, I cannot remember all of it. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Osman Hasanagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He also disappeared on Vlasic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Vasif Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Vasif Mujkanovic also went missing in 1992. I believe that he was with this convoy carrying 250 people on the Vlasic mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Dzevad Besic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. Dzevad Besic was a forester. He also went missing. I don't know the circumstances of his disappearance, but I know that he never showed up again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Hamdija Avdagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, Hamdija Avdagic as I said, he disappeared in Kozarac(redacted) (redacted) Nijaz Memic, a football player from Kozarac who disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Sakib Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. He spent entire time in the white house, but he used to work in the mine complex, that is, in the compound where we were detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Suad Besic, otherwise known as Dudo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Dudo, yes, I know him. He, too, disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, I think we need to redact on page 60, lines 24 and 25. Or just line 25, the first three words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On my computer, it's starting already 24, 25. The sentence may be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of a person called Fadil Colic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, Fadil Colic owned a car repair shop, a Mercedes workshop before the war. He lived at Urije, a neighbourhood situated between Kamicani and Kevljani in the direction of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of his fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: All I know is that he's missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Sead Crnic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Sead Crnic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He's from Kozarusa. He used to play the guitar in a local band. He disappeared in Kozarac, but I am not familiar with the circumstances of his disappearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Akib Deumic otherwise known as Pcelica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned him. Akib Deumic, also known as Pcelica, he used to be a member of the police force. He went missing in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Muhamed Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes. He was a cook. He worked in a restaurant in Kozarac. But he was also my bookkeeper. He used to help me in the kitchen as well, when he had time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of a person called Ahmed Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: He's from Kozarusa. He also disappeared sometime in 1992. I don't know exactly how, but he was not in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Suad Jakupovic, otherwise known as Sudo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: That day, he was singled out at the checkpoint in Kozarusa. He remained in the space which we called a tin container. I think that Commander Prpus from Prijedor is his brother-in-law or is otherwise related to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he is still alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know, or he's not alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No, he never came back. Since that day in 1992, he has never reappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session to ask the witness some information about his property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections, so therefore private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be provided with the B/C/S version of Exhibit 130, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence is in possession of this document in B/C/S as well, in order to crosscheck?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's Number 190 from the Rule 65 ter list. We have a spare copy if you would like one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you need a spare copy for your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read the document that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, it's a document signed by Simo Drljaca, the chief of the SJB in Prijedor. Communication number 11-12-2031, dated 29 May, 1992. It's addressed to the Banja Luka CSB. And the subject of the document is: "Re: Your communication number 11-2709-401," dated 28 May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As a question of principle, this document, can you check on your database whether or not, for example, this document is available in an original? We'll see that it might be a copy, but having a signature, say, in blue or dark and on the top of the page, the numbering, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or is it limited to photocopies only?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I can get what is the most original, whatever document is in the evidence unit that has this ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier that a large number of policemen were detained in the collection centres and were either killed or disappeared in 1992. Could you please read out for the Court paragraph number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be even more kind and read the entire document for us, that we understand the context of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the basis of your communication of the above number and date, we hereby submit to you the following details: Firstly, in Prijedor, there is one police station with general authority with three branch stations; Omarska police department, Kozarac police department, and Ljubija police department. "Before the conflict broke out, there were 107 active policemen, 26 of them from the Kozarac area. A number of these policemen were killed in combat operations, and the others are in the collection centre. "The following command posts have been filled: Prijedor police station commander, two deputy commanders, and two commanders of branch stations. Vacant posts: One deputy commander, one assistant commander, and one branch station commander. Kozarac police department. "Following combat activities, the minimum number of policemen required to complete duties and tasks successfully should be between 150 and 180. "There is a police station for road safety and traffic control in Prijedor. "This station currently has 32 posts and 20 police officers to fill them. "The commander of the station is in Bosanska Gradiska prison. The deputy commander runs the station, while the assistant is in the collection centre. "The new war structure anticipates 13 police stations, plus the police station for road safety and traffic control. "The war structure anticipates 1.342 members in general police stations, and 52 members in the road safety station. Of that number 1.214 should be reserve, and 180 active police officers. "The previous war structure anticipated 630 policemen. The new war structure, which is functioning now, was prepared during secret preparations for the takeover. It is believed that this war structure can ensure the successful performance of police duties and tasks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the final paragraph where it reads: "The new war structure which is functioning now was prepared during secret preparations for the takeover."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: Secret, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any preparations before the takeover occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS R
utterances.text: No. I wasn't familiar with any of the communiques or rather incoming documents to the police station before the takeover. I didn't have any insight into these matters. I was only in the reserve component of the police force. So I had no access to such documents. And after all, this document was drafted when I was already in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, may we ask you to return tomorrow. Then the Defence will have some additional questions, and also the Judges. For today, you are excused. Thank you very much. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 3.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've located the original of Prosecution Exhibit S130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it could be presented to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've shown it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we also have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The signature is in blue ink, and the reference number at the top of the document is also in blue ink. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the stamp with registration number P following can be seen in red, just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like the Office of the Prosecutor to obtain a colour photocopy of that so you can see the difference, the blue ink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That would be great indeed. Yes. We have to conclude our work. It's still open. You tendered this document S130A and B. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only again, we cannot confirm the signature of Simo Drljaca. Otherwise, we don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore and thereby, this document, former 190, is admitted into evidence under Number 130A for the English version, B for the French version. And please, registry, add to this document that it was read out on today's transcript, 10 June, 2002, on pages 71 following.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be 130B for the B/C/S, and 130C for the French version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We don't -- do we have really a French version already?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is what is in the transcript, Your Honour. You said 130B for the French version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. A for English, B for B/C/S. And just to know that we have a rough translation on the transcript, page 71 following in today's transcript. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the registry acts extremely careful. And I was told that one videoclip, you remember it was a very short one with a speech of Mr. Karadzic, tendered under number S117 was not yet admitted. Are there any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I remember properly, it's a few seconds clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I don't know if we have it. So if there is a complete version of that video, so we can see what's coming after it or what we have before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence has the longer tape that that's a part of. It was disclosed on the 25th of March. It's from the videotape that is excerpts from the "Death of Yugoslavia" programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this is admitted into evidence as number S117. This clip shown on that day only. Then during the break, not knowing yet about the outcome of our more or less admittedly fishing expedition on the "most original document" as regards S130, we conferred during the break and hereby order as follows: All the documents included in Exhibit 54, this is list 2, and 55, this is list 3, where reference is made to alleged authenticity of a document of Dr. Stakic, be it just a print in a newspaper or in the official gazette, be it a document without signature at all but giving at least the impression that this document was signed by Dr. Stakic, and documents signed -- documents where we still have not yet clarification on the authenticity, I refer to the transcript of last Friday, all these documents shall be presented by the OTP in the most original version in order to allow the Defence to come to a fair decision on their way deciding whether or not to comment on the one or other document. Of course, it has to be emphasised there's no duty at all for the Defence. It's, of course, the predominant right to remain silent. But nevertheless, it would also in the interests of justice and all the Judges would like to see these documents in the most appropriate way. We received the Prosecution's third notice for admission of transcripts and statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis dated 7 June, 2002 proposing that the written statements of another six witnesses should be admitted into evidence under this rule. We regard it as adequate, taking into account that we sit the entire day from Monday through Thursday, to discuss and come to a conclusion no later but Monday, 17 June, 2002. This should not be confused with that what I announced earlier this day, that is, rethinking of former statements admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis already in the past, but with a view to the Appeals Chamber's decision. Here, we expect the observations of the parties no later than Monday, 8 July. Furthermore, I learned by the registry that Document 59 was not yet admitted into evidence. It was tendered. And it's our intention to proceed as follows: That at least most of the documents to be found in these lists 2 and 3, there should be as soon as possible access for all the Judges, first of all, at the same time, and at the same time, it should be safeguarded that the Defence has a possibility to view whether or not they believe that the translation in the one or other point may be inappropriate. Therefore, the intention is to start to read out these documents in the courtroom. And could we please start with Document 59 in the English version. And it's free for the parties to comment on this document by document, both to the content and to the translation. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Serbian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, do the interpreters have originals of these documents or B/C/S translations? Are we expected to do a sight translation of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course not. The booth needs two copies or how many? How many documents are needed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One copy, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just make one comment. It really doesn't make sense to me to check the translation of this document being read from English into B/C/S when we have the B/C/S original. The original is in B/C/S. I understand the purpose of this is so we have a French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a French translation, and at the same time to give the Defence the opportunity to object to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have a certified translation the Defence has had for quite some time on all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I think you are aware that the one or other point was made by the Defence as regards translation. It was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only to point out that this is the appropriate time to make any such comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have those documents in our locker here, but we don't have it with us. We don't drag these trolleys with us every day. So we have to decide what to bring to the courtroom, and we didn't know we are going to deal with this. If you allow my case manager just to go and fetch our binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we have two copies. You can borrow mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But we have to give our copy to the translation booth, so we are short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the meantime, are there any other observations by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As to the 92 bis and the decision of the 7th of June on the Galic case, I've read that decision, and it's consistent with our view of the rule. Our position has not changed on any of the 92 bis submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's only fair to give also the Defence to rethink this in the light of the new decision. I am not surprised by your view, but I think it's only fair. utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina government. Excerpt from instructions for the work of the municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people. One, in a state of war, the Crisis Staff shall assume all prerogatives and functions of the Municipal Assemblies when they are unable to convene. "Two, the Crisis Staff consists of members, each of whom has his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. own responsibilities. The president, deputy president, commander of the TO, Territorial Defence staff, president of the executive committee, head of Ministry of the Interior, and members responsible for the economy, humanitarian, medical care, information, and propaganda, procurement and food supplies, refugees, war crimes, and damage, communications, coordination, et cetera. "Three, the Crisis Staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence of the territories, the safety of the population and property, the establishment of government, and the organisation of all other areas of life and work. In so doing, the Crisis Staff provides the conditions for the municipal executive committee to exercise legal executive authority, run the economy, and other areas of life. "Four, the command of the TO and police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff, and therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented. "Five, ban the use of all artillery seized in combat or acquired by other means which can be used to destroy towns and remove it far from the confrontation line. "Six, the work of the Crisis Staff is based on constitutional and legal provisions and on decisions reached by the assembly, the presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Seven, the Crisis Staff shall convene a meeting of the Municipal Assembly as soon as circumstances permit to have its work, conclusions, and decisions verified. "Eight, the Crisis Staff has the obligation to provide working and living conditions for JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, members to ensure a fair attitude towards JNA officers and soldiers, and prevent them from being humiliated or insulted in any way. As far as the attitude towards army property is concerned, it must be based on obligatory consultations of the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Nine, the Crisis Staff shall provide working conditions for the international peace and relief organisations and ensure the unimpeded transport of relief convoys to their destinations. "Ten, the nonfighting population and the wounded must be treated in the most humane fashion and in accordance with the ICRC. Prisoners of war also must be treated humanely and in accordance with the rules of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Eleven, the Crisis Staff shall gather information concerning the field situation and to inform and consult the competent bodies of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina i.e., the government commissioners appointed to the area especially threatened by war. " 12, it is imperative not to disturb commercial and other economic activities, as long as their documentation is in order. Prices must be formed at a level which enables normal function. If necessary, limit the prices of basic food stuffs, bread, butter, sugar and oil, and subsequently introduce food rationing for the above-mentioned articles. 13, war profiteers, gangs of looters, and similar shall be arrested and delivered to the investigating judicial organs of the Serbian Republic. 14 The Crisis Staff shall convene and make decisions in the presence of all its members, take official minutes, issue written decisions and submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Sarajevo, 26 April, 1992, prime minister, Branko Dzeric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Defence once more about observation -- objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.text: Handwritten: "PS2-?29. 434, pursuant to the decision of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the general public mobilisation of forces and materiel in the republic, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality, considering the current situation and conditions at the meeting held on 22nd of May, 1992, reached a decision on mobilisation on the territory of Prijedor Municipality. utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "One, general provisions. These instructions serve to determine the establishment, composition, appointment, rights and duties of the local Crisis Staffs and their relations with other institutions and to designate the territory for which a local Crisis Staff is formed. "Two, the local Crisis Staffs are to be set up for the territory of two or more local communes as temporary organs of civilian authority in that territory with all the powers of the regularly elected organs. "Three, in addition to ex officio members, primarily persons who are completely loyal and committed to the policy and direction taken by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and enjoy great respect and trust in their own communities while possessing the creative abilities and determination necessary for such complex and responsible tasks, shall be considered for appointments to the local Crisis Staff. "Four, members of the local Crisis Staffs are to be appointed by the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff after receiving prior recommendations and opinions from the local communes whose territory is to be under the jurisdiction of that local Crisis Staff. "Five, the following local Crisis Staffs are to be set up in the Prijedor Municipality. One, the Prijedor centre local Crisis Staff for the territory of local communes. Prijedor centre, Prijedor III. Two, the Prijedor II local Crisis Staff for the territory of the local communes. Prijedor II, Cirkin Polje. Three, the Omarska local Crisis Staff for the territory of local communes, Omarska, Gradina, Lamovita, Maricka, Petrov Gaj, and Kevljani. Five, the Brezicani local Crisis Staff for the territory of local communes, Brezicani, D. Dragontinja, G. Dragontinja, Jutragosta, Cejreci. Six, the Palanciste local Crisis Staff for the territory of local communes: Palanciste, Jelovac, Bozici, and G. Orlovci. Seven, the Ljubija local Crisis Staff for the territory of local communes: Ljubija, Donja Ljubija, Gornji Ravska, Surkovac, Miska Glava, Ljeskare, and Volar.
